title: "Checking Local Files with repo_check and code_check"

---




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(metacheck)
```
:::


## Overview

Metacheck has two modules that work together to check research code:

- **`repo_check`** lists all files in a repository and checks for basic
  organisational quality: is there a README? Are there archives whose contents
  cannot be listed? Do the file names follow good practice, and are there files
  that do not belong in a repository? How many code, data, and other files are
  there?

- **`code_check`** reads the actual code files and checks them for
  best-practice issues: comments, absolute file paths, `setwd()` and
  `install.packages()` calls, grouped library loading, missing data files,
  code that cannot be parsed, and whether the package versions are recorded.

Normally both modules fetch files automatically from online repositories (OSF,
GitHub, GitLab, ResearchBox, Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, and several
others — see [Repository Check](mod-repo-check.qmd) for the full list) by
following links found in a paper. This vignette shows how to point them at a
**local folder** instead — useful when:

- you want to check your own code before sharing it
- you are reviewing a paper whose files were sent as a zip attachment
- you downloaded a repository's files yourself, or the authors used a
  repository service Metacheck does not support automatically

::: callout-tip
If you just want a report on a folder — no manuscript involved — `report_repository()` wraps the pattern this chapter walks through by hand: give it a path, and it runs `repo_check`, `code_check`, `data_check`, and `codebook_check` on it and writes a report named after the folder. See [Downloading OSF files to check locally](#downloading-osf-files-to-check-locally) below for an example, and [Creating a Report](creating-a-report.qmd) for the full function reference.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Without R
[Metacheck's website](https://metacheckserve.metacheck.src.surf-hosted.nl/) checks a local folder too: under *Run Metacheck on a Repository*, choose the folder or a .zip file, and it runs `repo_check`, `code_check`, and `data_check`, and can also run the R and Python code. The folder is then uploaded to the server, which deletes it once it has been read. To keep files on your own computer, for example files sent to you for review, use the [Docker installation](get-started.qmd#docker-installation), which offers the same website locally.
:::

---

## Before you start

Load the package and note the path format for your operating system:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(metacheck)
```
:::


| Operating system | Example path |
|---|---|
| Windows | `"C:/Users/researcher/Documents/my_study"` |
| macOS / Linux | `"/Users/researcher/Documents/my_study"` |

Both forward slashes `/` and backslashes `\\` work on Windows inside R.

When you provide a local path, the folder is treated as a repository in
exactly the same way as an OSF project or GitHub repo. Each folder is a
repository of its own, named by its path in the `repo_url` column of the file
table. The summary table has one row per paper, however many folders you
check, and the module gives one traffic light for all of them together.

---

## Part 1: `repo_check` on local files

### What `repo_check` checks

For each folder you provide, `repo_check` will:

- **List all files** and classify them by type (code, data, archive, readme, ...)
- **Check for a README** — a README file is good practice and helps others
  understand the contents of a folder
- **Look inside zip archives** — the files inside a `.zip` file are listed in
  place of the archive. Other archive formats, such as `.7z`, `.rar` or
  `.tar.gz`, cannot be listed this way, so `repo_check` flags them and
  recommends `.zip`
- **Check file names** — for example names or paths that are too long, or
  characters that cause problems on some computers
- **Flag files that do not belong in a repository** — files that software
  creates by itself, such as `.DS_Store`, `.Rhistory` or editor backups, and
  version-control or editor folders such as `.git/`. They are left out of the
  file list and named in the report
- **Report counts** — how many code files, data files, and so on

The traffic light is `"red"` when the folder holds files that software creates
by itself (such as `.DS_Store` or `.Rhistory`). It is `"green"` when every
repository has a README, no archive is left that could not be listed, every
file could be classified, no file name breaks a naming rule, there are no
version-control or editor folders, every repository could be read, and (when
there is a manuscript) the studies it names match how the files are grouped.
Otherwise it is `"yellow"`.

### Checking a single folder


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
repo <- module_run(test_paper(), "repo_check",
                   local_path = "C:/projects/reaction_time_study_2024")

# Plain-text summary
repo$summary_text

# Summary counts (one row per paper)
repo$summary_table

# "green", "yellow" or "red"
repo$traffic_light

# Full file list — one row per file, with file_type and file_size columns
repo$table
```
:::


`test_paper()` creates a minimal paper object with no repository links. The
module pipeline always requires a paper argument, but when you are only
checking a local folder there is no manuscript — `test_paper()` gives you a
valid object that causes the online repository search to find nothing, so only
the local files are checked.

> **Note on cloud-sync folders (OneDrive, iCloud, Dropbox):** If the folder
> is stored online and files have not been downloaded locally, the check will
> be slow because each code file triggers a download when it is read. Before
> running, right-click the folder in your file browser and choose
> **"Always keep on this device"** (OneDrive) or **"Download Now"** (iCloud)
> to make all files available locally first.

A typical `$summary_text` when the folder is missing a README might look like:

```
- We found 8 files in 1 repository.
- We found 0 README files and 1 repository without READMEs.
```

And `$summary_table` will have columns: `paper_id`, `repo_n`,
`repo_unchecked`, `files_n`, `files_data`, `files_code`, `files_readme`,
`files_zip`, `files_unknown`, `naming_issues`, `roster_mismatch`.

### Checking multiple folders

Pass a vector of paths to check several folders at once. Each is treated as a
separate repository. The summary table still has one row, for the one paper,
with `repo_n` counting the folders; the file table names each file's folder in
`repo_url`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
paths <- c(
  "C:/projects/study_1_power_analysis",
  "C:/projects/study_2_replication",
  "C:/projects/study_3_meta_analysis"
)

repo <- module_run(test_paper(), "repo_check", local_path = paths)

# One row, with repo_n = 3
repo$summary_table

# All files from all three folders, with repo_url identifying the source
repo$table

# Number of files of each type (code, data, readme, ...) per folder
table(repo$table$repo_url, repo$table$file_type)
```
:::


This is a quick way to compare whether several projects all have READMEs and
no archives that cannot be listed before you submit or share them.

---

## Part 2: `code_check` on local files

### What `code_check` checks

`code_check` builds on `repo_check`: it first runs the file inventory, then
reads every code file (R, Rmd, Qmd, Python and Jupyter notebooks, SAS, SPSS,
Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB; JASP files are counted but not read) and checks for:

- **Comments** — is the code explained? A file with no comment lines at all
  is flagged.
- **Absolute paths** — paths like `C:/myname/files/data.csv` only work on
  one specific computer and will break for anyone else trying to reproduce
  the analysis.
- **`setwd()` and `install.packages()` calls** — `setwd()` ties the script to
  one computer's folders, and `install.packages()` installs software on the
  computer of whoever runs the script, without asking.
- **Library loading** — are all `library()` / `require()` calls grouped
  together near the top of the script, or are they scattered throughout?
- **Missing data files** — if the script loads `read.csv("data.csv")` but
  `data.csv` is not in the folder, that is flagged.
- **Parsing** — can the R code (`.R`, `.Rmd`, `.qmd`) be read without syntax
  errors?
- **Recorded package versions** — is there an `renv.lock` file, a
  `sessionInfo()` record, or a `groundhog`/`checkpoint` call for R code, and a
  package list such as `requirements.txt` for Python code?

### Checking your own code

You have finished a project and want to review the quality of your scripts
before sharing:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
result <- module_run(test_paper(), "code_check",
                     local_path = "C:/projects/reaction_time_study_2024")

# Short summary of all findings
result$summary_text

# One row per code file with detailed metrics
result$table

# "green" (no issues), "yellow" (some issues), or "na" (no code files read)
result$traffic_light

# Full formatted report
result$report
```
:::


> **Note on cloud-sync folders:** If your files are on OneDrive, iCloud, or
> another cloud-sync service and are not fully downloaded, the check will be
> slow, because every file has to be downloaded when it is read; Metacheck
> does not warn you about this. Right-click the folder and choose
> "Always keep on this device" (OneDrive) or "Download Now" (iCloud) before
> running the check.

### Checking multiple projects


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
paths <- c(
  "C:/projects/study_1_power_analysis",
  "C:/projects/study_2_replication",
  "C:/projects/study_3_meta_analysis"
)

result <- module_run(test_paper(), "code_check", local_path = paths)

result$summary_text

# Filter to one folder using dplyr
library(dplyr)

result$table |>
  filter(grepl("study_2", repo_url)) |>
  select(file_name, percentage_comment, code_abs_path, loaded_files_missing)
```
:::


The `repo_url` column contains the folder path, so you can always identify
which folder a code file came from. Every code file in a folder is checked.

### Peer review — files sent as a zip archive

When reviewing a paper, authors sometimes supply code and data as a zip file
attached to the submission. Once you unzip it, you have a local folder:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# After unzipping the submission to a folder:
result <- module_run(test_paper(), "code_check",
                     local_path = "C:/peer_review/garcia_2024_submission")

result$report   # copy this into your review
```
:::


### Code hosted on an unsupported repository

Metacheck currently retrieves files automatically from **OSF, GitHub,
GitLab, ResearchBox, PsychArchives and other DSpace repositories, Zenodo,
Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE,
and LDbase**. Other services, such as Bitbucket or Google Drive, are not
supported. If the paper links to one of these, download the files manually
and point `code_check` at the downloaded folder.

The workflow is the same for all of them:

1. Go to the link in the paper
2. Download the files (usually a "Download all" button, or clone with git)
3. Unzip if needed
4. Run `code_check`


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Author shared code on Bitbucket — you downloaded or cloned it locally
result <- module_run(test_paper(), "code_check",
                     local_path = "C:/downloads/lee_2023_bitbucket_code")

result$summary_text
result$traffic_light
```
:::


---

## Part 3: Combining a paper with local files

Sometimes a paper links to an online repository that Metacheck supports, but
there are also supplementary files that were shared separately — for example,
the main data is on OSF but additional analysis scripts were sent as a zip by
the editor. You can check both at once:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
paper <- read("garcia_2024.pdf")

# repo_check fetches the OSF files AND lists the local folder
result <- module_run(paper, "code_check",
                 local_path = "C:/peer_review/garcia_2024_extra_scripts")

# Online files have a URL in repo_url; local files have the folder path
unique(result$table$repo_url)
```
:::


`repo_check` treats the online repository and the local folder as two
repositories. The summary table counts both in one row for the paper, and the
`repo_url` column of the file table shows which files, README files, and
archives are in the online repo and which in the local folder:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
repo <- module_run(paper, "repo_check",
                   local_path = "C:/peer_review/garcia_2024_extra_scripts")

# One row for the paper, with repo_n = 2 (the OSF project and the local folder)
repo$summary_table
repo$traffic_light

# Number of files of each type per repository
table(repo$table$repo_url, repo$table$file_type)
```
:::


---

## Part 4: Running `repo_check` and `code_check` as a two-step pipeline

By default, `code_check` runs `repo_check` internally and you do not see its
output. If you want to inspect the file inventory before the code analysis, or
save the `repo_check` results separately, run them as two steps. When you pass
a `repo_check` result as the first argument to `code_check`, the file list is
reused — the folder is not re-read:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
path <- "C:/projects/reaction_time_study_2024"

# Step 1: inventory and organisational checks
repo <- module_run(test_paper(), "repo_check", local_path = path)

repo$summary_text    # how many files, README present?
repo$traffic_light   # green / yellow
repo$table           # full file list with types and sizes

# Step 2: code quality analysis (reuses the file list from step 1)
code <- module_run(repo, "code_check")

code$summary_text    # code-specific summary
code$table           # one row per code file
code$traffic_light
```
:::


This is especially useful when the folder is on a cloud-sync drive: any slow
file downloads happen once (during `code_check`), not twice.

---

## Understanding the output

### `repo_check` output

| Element | What it contains |
|---|---|
| `$traffic_light` | `"green"` (no issues), `"yellow"` (issues, such as a missing README or an archive that cannot be listed), `"red"` (files that software creates by itself, such as `.DS_Store`), or `"na"` (no repos) |
| `$summary_text` | Plain-text summary: file counts, README status, archives, file names, files that do not belong |
| `$summary_table` | One row per paper: `paper_id`, `repo_n`, `repo_unchecked`, `files_n`, `files_data`, `files_code`, `files_readme`, `files_zip`, `files_unknown`, `naming_issues`, `roster_mismatch` |
| `$table` | One row per file, with columns including `paper_id`, `repo_url`, `file_name`, `file_path`, `file_url`, `file_location`, `file_size`, `file_type`, and `group` (the study a file belongs to) |
| `$report` | Formatted report explaining any README, archive, file-name, or other issues |

### `code_check` output

| Element | What it contains |
|---|---|
| `$traffic_light` | `"green"` (no issues), `"yellow"` (issues found), or `"na"` (no code files read) |
| `$summary_text` | Plain-text summary of all checks across all files |
| `$summary_table` | One row per paper: `paper_id`, `code_n`, `code_checked`, `code_abs_path`, `code_setwd`, `code_install_packages`, `code_missing_files`, `code_min_comments`, `code_parse_errors`, `code_packages_n`, `code_version_pinned` |
| `$table` | One row per code file with detailed metrics (see below) |
| `$report` | Full formatted report suitable for pasting into a review |

Key columns in `code_check`'s `$table`:

| Column | What it means |
|---|---|
| `file_name` | Script filename |
| `repo_url` | Which folder (or online repo) the file came from |
| `language` | Detected language: R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB, or JASP |
| `percentage_comment` | Share of non-blank lines that are comments (0 = no comments at all) |
| `loaded_files_missing` | Number of data files the script tries to load that are not in the folder |
| `loaded_files_missing_names` | The names of those missing files |
| `code_abs_path` | Number of absolute file paths detected |
| `library_max_between` | Largest gap in lines between consecutive `library()` calls |

---

## Downloading OSF files to check locally

Often the files you want to check live in an OSF project rather than on your own disk. You can download them first, then point `repo_check` / `code_check` at the downloaded folder using the local-file options above.

OSF projects let you organise information into nested components, and files within those components. To retrieve all of the files associated with a project by hand, you may need to navigate to several components, download a zip for each, then reorganise and rename the downloaded folders.

The function `osf_file_download()` does all of this for you, recreating a folder structure based on the component names. By default (`mode = "all"`) it fetches every component's files as a single compressed archive per component, with no size filtering — `max_file_size` and `max_download_size` are both `NULL` (no limit) by default, and neither one applies in this mode, because there is no file list to filter against. To filter by size instead, pass `mode = "select"`, which lists every file individually through the OSF API before downloading, and only then applies `max_file_size`/`max_download_size` (in megabytes). See the [Archiving OSF Files](archiving-osf.qmd) appendix for the full comparison between the two modes, and for `report_repository()`, which can take over from here once the files are on disk.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
osf_file_download(osf_id = "pngda",
                  download_to = ".",
                  mode = "select",
                  max_file_size = 1,
                  max_download_size = 10)
```
:::


```
Starting retrieval for pngda
- omitting metacheck.png (1.5MB)
Downloading files [=====================] 24/24 00:00:35
```

The files are written into a folder named after the OSF id, preserving the project's nested structure:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
list.files("pngda", recursive = TRUE)
```
:::

```

```
:::


Once downloaded, you can run the checks on that folder exactly as shown earlier:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
module_run(test_paper(), "code_check", local_path = "pngda", local_only = TRUE)
```
:::


Or, since there is no manuscript involved at this point, skip the manual `test_paper()`/`module_run()` steps and call `report_repository()` instead, which runs `repo_check`, `code_check`, `data_check`, and `codebook_check` on the folder in one step and writes a report named after it:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
report_repository("pngda")
```
:::
